query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Ti to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) can improve the strength-ductility combination by increasing grain boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with low plasticity at room temperature
generation.mechanism: Increased grain boundary cohesion leads to improved plasticity and strength
generation.boundary: Limited to refractory high-entropy alloys with specific compositions
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of Ti addition on grain boundary cohesion and strength-ductility combination is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical properties of RHEAs with and without Ti addition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Ti does not lead to improved strength-ductility combination, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
